questions.question: Describe the relationship between kinetic energy and potential energy as the object falls.
marking_criteria: Describe the change in kinetic energy as the object falls.
Describe the change in potential energy as the object falls.
Explain the relationship between the changes in kinetic and potential energy.
hints: Look at the changes in kinetic and potential energy values at different heights.
questions.model_answer: As the object falls, kinetic energy increases while potential energy decreases. At the start (12 m), the object has maximum potential energy and zero kinetic energy. As it falls, potential energy is converted into kinetic energy. At the bottom (0 m), the object has maximum kinetic energy and zero potential energy. The sum of kinetic and potential energy remains constant at 1200 J.
questions.explanation: Describe how kinetic and potential energy change as the object falls and explain their relationship.

questions.scenario: Refer to the diagram showing a simple pendulum with a bob of mass m attached to a rigid support by a thread of length L. The pendulum is released from rest at an angle θ from the vertical.
questions.question: Calculate the speed of the bob at the mean position if it is released from an angle θ = 30°.
marking_criteria: Identify that at mean position, KE = PE lost from release height.
State PE at release = mgL(1 − cos θ); KE at mean = ½mv².
Apply conservation: mgL(1 − cos 30°) = ½mv².
Solve for v: v = √(2gL(1 − cos 30°)).
Substitute cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866 to get v ≈ √(2gL × 0.134) or v ≈ 1.28√(gL) [accept symbolic or numerical form].
hints: Stay focused on this: Calculate the speed of the bob at the mean position if it is released from an angle θ = 30° — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: Apply mgL(1 − cos 30°) = ½mv².; Solve for v: v = √(2gL(1 − cos 30°)).
questions.model_answer: At the mean position, PE = 0. At release (angle 30°), height above mean is h = L(1 − cos 30°). By conservation of energy: mgL(1 − cos 30°) = ½mv². Solving: v = √(2gL(1 − cos 30°)). Since cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866, we have v = √(2gL × 0.134) ≈ 1.28√(gL). If L is given, substitute to find numerical value.
questions.explanation: Use the conservation of energy principle to find the speed of the bob at the mean position. Start by equating the potential energy at the highest point to the kinetic energy at the mean position.

questions.scenario: Refer to the diagram showing a simple pendulum with a bob of mass m attached to a rigid support by a thread of length L. The pendulum is released from rest at an angle θ from the vertical.
questions.question: Explain why the period of the pendulum is independent of the mass of the bob.
marking_criteria: Correctly state the formula for the period of a simple pendulum.
Explain why the mass term cancels out in the formula.
hints: Stay focused on this: Explain why the period of the pendulum is independent of the mass of the bob — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: why the mass term cancels out in the.
questions.model_answer: The period of a simple pendulum is given by T = 2π√(L/g). Notice that the mass m does not appear in this formula. Therefore, the period is independent of the mass of the bob.
questions.explanation: Explain why the period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the mass of the bob by referring to the formula for the period.

questions.model_answer: To determine the length of the pendulum, use a meter stick to measure the distance from the rigid support to the center of the bob. questions.scenario: Refer to the diagram showing two rows of circuit diagrams, each showing a series of three steps. The top row (Diagram A) has a battery, a 3Ω resistor and a 5Ω resistor, plus two parallel 6Ω resistors; this reduces to a circuit with 3Ω, 5Ω and an unknown '???' resistor, then to a battery with a single '???' resistor. Diagram B has a battery, a 9Ω and a 5Ω resistor, plus a 12Ω and a 6Ω resistor in parallel; this reduces to 9Ω, 5Ω and '???', then to a battery with a single '???' resistor.
questions.question: Calculate the equivalent resistance of the circuit in Diagram A when the two parallel 6Ω resistors are combined into a single resistor.
marking_criteria: Correctly identify the parallel resistors (6Ω, 6Ω).
Calculate the equivalent resistance of the parallel resistors.
Combine the equivalent resistance of the parallel resistors with the series resistors (3Ω, 5Ω) to find the total equivalent resistance.

questions.model_answer: The equivalent resistance of the two parallel 6Ω resistors is calculated as 1/R_eq = 1/6Ω + 1/6Ω = 1/3Ω, so R_eq = 3Ω. The total equivalent resistance of the circuit is then 3Ω + 5Ω + 3Ω = 11Ω.
questions.explanation: First, find the equivalent resistance of the two parallel resistors, then add this to the series resistors to find the total equivalent resistance of the circuit.

questions.scenario: Refer to the diagram showing two rows of circuit diagrams, each showing a series of three steps. The top row (Diagram A) has a battery, a 3Ω resistor and a 5Ω resistor, plus two parallel 6Ω resistors; this reduces to a circuit with 3Ω, 5Ω and an unknown '???' resistor, then to a battery with a single '???' resistor. Diagram B has a battery, a 9Ω and a 5Ω resistor, plus a 12Ω and a 6Ω resistor in parallel; this reduces to 9Ω, 5Ω and '???', then to a battery with a single '???' resistor.
questions.question: Explain why the equivalent resistance of the circuit in Diagram B is higher than that in Diagram A.
marking_criteria: Calculate equivalent resistance of parallel resistors in Diagram B: 1/R_eq = 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/4, so R_eq = 4Ω.
Calculate total equivalent resistance in Diagram B: 9Ω + 5Ω + 4Ω = 18Ω.
Compare totals: Diagram B (18Ω) is higher than Diagram A (11Ω) because the parallel combination in B (4Ω) is larger than in A (3Ω), and the series resistors in B are also larger (9Ω vs 3Ω).
hints: Address the full question in a clear chain of reasoning — not a single short statement.
questions.model_answer: In Diagram A, the equivalent resistance is 11Ω (as calculated in part a). In Diagram B, the 12Ω and 6Ω resistors in parallel give: 1/R_eq = 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/4, so R_eq = 4Ω. The total equivalent resistance in Diagram B is 9Ω + 5Ω + 4Ω = 18Ω. Diagram B has higher equivalent resistance because both its series resistors (9Ω and 5Ω) are larger than those in Diagram A (3Ω and 5Ω), and its parallel combination (4Ω) is larger than Diagram A's (3Ω).
questions.explanation: The higher initial resistors and their configuration in Diagram B lead to a higher equivalent resistance compared to Diagram A.

questions.scenario: Refer to the diagram showing a 2 kg block sliding down a frictionless inclined plane from a height of 8 metres. The diagram includes bar charts showing the kinetic energy (KE) and potential energy (PE) at different positions along the plane.
questions.question: Calculate the total mechanical energy of the block at the top of the inclined plane.
marking_criteria: Correctly identify potential energy using the formula PE = mgh.
State that kinetic energy is zero at the top.
Sum the potential energy and kinetic energy to find the total mechanical energy.
hints: Use the mass of the block and the height to calculate potential energy.
questions.model_answer:
PE = mgh = 2 kg * 9.8 m/s^2 * 8 m = 156.8 J
Total Mechanical Energy = PE + KE = 156.8 J + 0 J = 156.8 J
questions.explanation: Calculate the potential energy using the mass, gravitational acceleration, and height. Since the block is at rest at the top, its kinetic energy is zero.

questions.question: Explain why the total mechanical energy remains constant if there are no dissipative forces acting on the block.
marking_criteria: State the principle of conservation of mechanical energy.
Explain that in the absence of dissipative forces, energy is conserved.
Describe the transformation between kinetic and potential energy.
hints: Stay focused on this: Explain why the total mechanical energy remains constant if there are no dissipative forces acting on the block — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: the transformation between and energy.
questions.model_answer: The total mechanical energy remains constant because of the conservation of mechanical energy principle. In the absence of dissipative forces like friction, there is no loss of energy, so the sum of kinetic and potential energy remains constant throughout the motion.
questions.explanation: Explain that the conservation of mechanical energy means energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transformed from potential to kinetic energy and vice versa.

questions.scenario: Consider a simple circuit with two resistors, R1 = 10 Ω and R2 = 20 Ω, connected in series to a 12 V battery. The current flowing through the circuit is measured to be 0.4 A.
questions.question: Explain why the current through each resistor is the same in a series circuit.
marking_criteria: State that in a series circuit, there is only one path for the current to flow.
Explain that since there is only one path, the current must be the same through all components.
Use the concept of charge conservation to support the explanation.
hints: Stay focused on this: Explain why the current through each resistor is the same in a series circuit — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: the concept of to support the explanation.
questions.model_answer: In a series circuit, the current is the same through each resistor because there is only one path for the current to flow. According to the principle of charge conservation, the same amount of charge must pass through each point in the circuit per unit time, hence the current is the same throughout.
questions.explanation: Explain the behaviour of current in a series circuit using the principle of charge conservation.

questions.scenario: Consider a simple circuit with two resistors, R1 = 10 Ω and R2 = 20 Ω, connected in series to a 12 V battery. The current flowing through the circuit is measured to be 0.4 A.
questions.question: Calculate the voltage drop across each resistor.
marking_criteria: Use Ohm's Law to find the voltage drop across R1.
Use Ohm's Law to find the voltage drop across R2.
Sum the voltage drops to ensure they equal the total voltage of the battery.
Show all steps and calculations clearly.
hints: Recall Ohm's Law: V = IR.
questions.model_answer: Voltage drop across R1, V1 = I * R1 = 0.4 A * 10 Ω = 4 V. Voltage drop across R2, V2 = I * R2 = 0.4 A * 20 Ω = 8 V. The sum of the voltage drops V1 + V2 = 4 V + 8 V = 12 V, which matches the total voltage of the battery.
questions.explanation: Use Ohm's Law to calculate the voltage drop across each resistor and verify that the sum of these drops equals the total voltage of the battery.

questions.question: Describe what would happen to the total mechanical energy if there were significant frictional forces present during the roller coaster car's descent.
marking_criteria: Correctly identifies the effect of frictional forces on mechanical energy (1 mark)
Correctly explains how frictional forces cause energy loss (1 mark)
Correctly describes the impact on total mechanical energy (1 mark)
hints: Address the full question in a clear chain of reasoning — not a single short statement.
questions.model_answer: If there were significant frictional forces present during the roller coaster car's descent, some of the mechanical energy would be converted into thermal energy due to friction. This would result in a loss of mechanical energy, meaning the total mechanical energy would decrease over time.
questions.explanation: Describe the impact of frictional forces on the total mechanical energy of the system.

questions.scenario: Refer to the diagram showing a 5 kg object attached to a spring with a spring constant k = 200 N/m, oscillating vertically. The object is displaced from its equilibrium position by 0.1 m and released.
questions.question: Calculate the total mechanical energy of the system at the moment of release.
marking_criteria: Correctly identify potential energy at maximum displacement.
Correctly identify kinetic energy at the moment of release.
Sum of potential and kinetic energy gives total mechanical energy.
hints: Use the formula for potential energy in a spring: PE = 0.5 * k * x^2.
questions.model_answer: PE = 0.5 * 200 N/m * (0.1 m)^2 = 1 J. Since the object is released from rest, KE = 0 J. Total mechanical energy = PE + KE = 1 J + 0 J = 1 J.
questions.explanation: Calculate the potential energy stored in the spring at maximum displacement and sum it with the kinetic energy, which is zero at the moment of release.

questions.question: Explain why the total mechanical energy remains constant throughout the oscillation in an ideal system without any dissipative forces.
marking_criteria: Correctly state the principle of conservation of mechanical energy.

hints: Stay focused on this: Explain why the total mechanical energy remains constant throughout the oscillation in an ideal system without any dissipative forces — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. questions.model_answer: In an ideal system without any dissipative forces, the total mechanical energy remains constant because there are no forces doing work to remove energy from the system. The mechanical energy is conserved and merely transforms between potential and kinetic energy.

questions.question: Describe how you would experimentally determine the period of the oscillation and relate it to the mass of the object and the spring constant.

Explain how to measure the period of oscillation.

questions.model_answer: To experimentally determine the period of oscillation, set up the oscillating system and release the object from the displaced position. questions.question: Explain why the voltage drop across each resistor is proportional to its resistance.
marking_criteria: State that in a series circuit, the current is the same through all resistors.
Explain that the voltage drop across a resistor is given by V = IR.
Conclude that the voltage drop is proportional to the resistance because I is constant.

questions.model_answer: In a series circuit, the current I is the same through all resistors. The voltage drop across a resistor is given by V = IR. Since I is constant, the voltage drop V is directly proportional to the resistance R.
questions.explanation: In a series circuit, the current is the same through all components. The voltage drop across each resistor is given by V = IR, where I is the current and R is the resistance. Since I is constant, the voltage drop is directly proportional to the resistance.

findings.detail: 4 questions open with the same sentence (12, 15, 24, 27): "Calculate the total resistance of the circuit."

issues.label: 2a
issues.detail: Model answer provides symbolic form v ≈ 1.28√(gL) but marking criteria require substitution of cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866. The calculation 2gL × 0.134 is correct (1 − 0.866 = 0.134), but the final symbolic answer should show v = √(2gL(1 − √3/2)) or v ≈ √(0.268gL) for consistency.
issues.correction: Model answer should state: v = √(2gL(1 − cos 30°)) = √(2gL(1 − √3/2)) = √(2gL × 0.134) ≈ 0.517√(gL) or approximately 1.28√(gL) if L and g are substituted numerically.

issues.label: 3b
issues.detail: Model answer states Diagram A has 3Ω series resistors, but the figure description shows 3Ω and 5Ω in series (not two 3Ω resistors). The calculation correctly uses 3Ω + 5Ω + 3Ω = 11Ω, but the explanation text is inconsistent with the circuit description.
issues.correction: Clarify: 'In Diagram A, the series resistors are 3Ω and 5Ω (not two 3Ω resistors). The parallel 6Ω resistors combine to 3Ω. Total: 3Ω + 5Ω + 3Ω = 11Ω.'

issues.label: 5a
issues.detail: Question 5a and 9a are identical (same context, same question, same answer). This violates the requirement to check for repeated questions with the same data.
issues.correction: Remove duplicate question 9a or replace with distinct circuit values/configuration.

issues.label: 5b
issues.detail: Question 5b and 9b are identical (same context, same question, same answer). This violates the requirement to check for repeated questions with the same data.
issues.correction: Remove duplicate question 9b or replace with distinct scenario.

issues.label: 5c
issues.detail: Question 5c and 9c are identical (same context, same question, same answer). This violates the requirement to check for repeated questions with the same data.
issues.correction: Remove duplicate question 9c or replace with distinct values.

issues.label: 4a
issues.detail: Model answer uses g = 9.8 m/s² but no context specifies this value. For Rwanda curriculum, g = 10 m/s² is standard. Using g = 10 m/s² gives PE = 2 × 10 × 8 = 160 J, not 156.8 J.
issues.correction: Either specify g = 9.8 m/s² in the question context or use g = 10 m/s² for PE = 160 J. Recommend g = 10 m/s² for grade 8 Rwanda curriculum.

issues.label: 2b
issues.detail: Model answer is incomplete. It states the formula T = 2π√(L/g) but does not explain why mass cancels out. The marking criteria require explanation of why mass term cancels, but the model answer does not derive or show this cancellation.
issues.correction: Expand model answer: 'The period formula T = 2π√(L/g) is derived from the balance of gravitational force and restoring force. The mass m appears in both the inertial term (ma) and gravitational term (mg), causing it to cancel algebraically, leaving only L and g.'

issues.label: 8c
issues.detail: Model answer does not explicitly relate the measured period to the formula T = 2π√(m/k) as required by marking criteria. It mentions the formula but does not explain how experimental data would be used to verify or derive it.
issues.correction: Add: 'Plot period T against √(m/k) to verify the linear relationship. The slope should equal 2π, confirming the formula T = 2π√(m/k).'

review.summary: Assessment contains substantive issues: three duplicate question sets (5a–5c repeated as 9a–9c), inconsistent gravitational acceleration value (9.8 vs 10 m/s²), incomplete model answers for pendulum period explanation (2b) and spring oscillation experiment (8c), and minor symbolic form inconsistency in pendulum speed calculation (2a). All topics fit curriculum; marking criteria are generally sound.
